question: It has recently been reported that a lack of judicial coordination has facilitated the escape of Karim Bouyakhrichan, leader of the well-known ‘Mocro Maffia’, or Moroccan Mafia, following his provisional release by the Provincial Court of Málaga in Spain. This individual is considered to be extremely dangerous.

He is also one of the most wanted criminals in the Netherlands for belonging to a criminal gang, drug trafficking and making death threats to Princess Amalia of Orange. The Netherlands filed an extradition request, but it was never executed. In view of this: 1.

Does the Commission consider it necessary to improve mechanisms for coordination and cooperation between Member States in order to ensure the effective implementation of the European arrest warrant and to prevent impunity for criminals wanted by different countries?
Is the Commission preparing an action plan to prevent the arrival of foreign criminal mafias in the European Union?
With regard to the Commission’s knowledge of other foreign mafias operating in the EU, in which regions do these mafias have the greatest presence?
answer: The European arrest warrant (EAW) framework decision is one of the most successful instruments of judicial cooperation in criminal matters and the Commission is working to make the EAW functioning as effectively as possible. The EAW is an entirely judicial procedure between judicial authorities in the Member States based on the particular circumstances of each individual case where surrender is requested.

Neither the Commission nor the Member States’ governments can interfere or influence decisions taken by judicial authorities. Nonetheless, the Commission monitors closely the transposition into national law of the framework decision on the EAW (1), including in Spain.
Since 2020, the Commission has launched infringement proceedings pursuant to Article 258 Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) where needed.

Moreover, the Commission released a new edition of the handbook on how to issue and execute an EAW (2) in November 2023 and publishes every year the EAW statistics based on information provided by the Member States acting both as issuing and as executing States (3).

Furthermore, building on the EU Strategy to tackle organised crime 2021-2025 (4), the EU Drugs Strategy and Action Plan 2021-2025 (5), the Commission adopted an EU Roadmap (6) to boost the fight against drug trafficking and organised crime on 18 October 2023 with concrete actions which will reinforce the EU’s global response.

One of the key actions of the Roadmap is the mapping of the most threatening criminal networks active in EU published by Europol in April 2024, providing extensive information on their activities, nationalities of members, modus operandi, their use of legal business structures, connections to other criminal networks and relations to other countries (7).
